clue.text: Passionate American twisted foot during pause, beginning to limp off

parts.note: a lull is a pause in the noise
the first letter of Limp — the L that LULL gives up
US for American and FT for foot, shaken together

explanation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations do the quiet work here: US for American and ft for foot. The letter that leaves is named by 'beginning to limp', so it is the pause word that gets trimmed, not the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustful means driven by desire, and 'passionate' covers the same heat — the carnal sense of passion rather than the enthusiast's.

clue.text: Tradesman avoids parking useless stuff

parts.note: the tradesman you call about pipes
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking — the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: P for parking comes off a road sign and setters use it constantly; the surface, with its tradesman dodging a meter, is pure misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: In British use lumber is disused clutter, the sort a lumber room holds, so 'useless stuff' names that junk sense rather than sawn timber.

clue.text: Busy parent very much taken by cricket club — more perturbed over master

parts.note: 'so' is very much, as in 'so much the better'
CC is the standard abbreviation for a cricket club
MORE with its letters perturbed
M is the abbreviation for master, as on a school timetable

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' means above rather than around, so the shuffled letters sit on top of the M instead of wrapping it.
explanation.definitionFit: A soccer mom is American shorthand for the suburban mother forever ferrying children to fixtures, so 'busy parent' names her by the schedule that defines her.

clue.text: Flustered state following drink

parts.note: f. is the reference-book abbreviation for 'following'
to lap is how a cat drinks

explanation.walkthrough: That f for following comes from indexes and footnotes, where 40f means page 40 and the one after — a small abbreviation setters lean on hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A flap is a panic — you are 'in a flap' — so the definition names the fluster itself, not the hinged cover that comes to mind first.

clue.text: Lingers over tucking into quantities of American wine

parts.note: litres in the American spelling — the measures wine comes in
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.walkthrough: 'American' is not part of the definition but a spelling instruction: it turns litres into LITERS, which is the only version with room for the O.
explanation.definitionFit: To loiter is to hang about longer than you need to, which is what 'lingers' catches — the same idle delay, with a hint of being up to no good.

clue.text: Stone interrupting ballet move? One may be letting off steam

definitions.text: One may be letting off steam

parts.note: a jeté is the leap where the dancer throws a leg out
the stone of a fruit is its pip

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark concedes the liberty in calling a pip a stone. Read 'letting off steam' literally too — no one here is losing their temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A jet pipe is the exhaust duct at the back of a jet engine, so it is the thing venting hot gas: steam let off in the physical sense.

clue.text: Avoiding politician, elected, though held in prison

parts.note: jug is old slang for prison
a Member of Parliament
a candidate who wins is in
surface only — it lets the sentence pretend the man is jailed despite winning his seat

explanation.walkthrough: Jug for prison is Victorian slang that survives mostly in crosswords, and 'held in' works twice over: the surface's custody and the instruction to insert.
explanation.definitionFit: To jump bail or jump a queue is to get past something you were meant to go through, so 'avoiding' names that dodging sense of the verb.

clue.text: Decide on a vocation to work the fast food till?

definitions.meaning: to take holy orders is to be ordained into the priesthood
the counter staff take what the customer asks for and ring it up

explanation.walkthrough: Holy orders and a burger counter are the two worlds the phrase lives in, and the clue slides from one to the other without a word of warning.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking holy orders is entering the priesthood — choosing a vocation — while taking orders at a counter is noting what customers want: one phrase, two callings.

clue.text: Struggles to get under one collection of invasive plants

parts.note: the Roman numeral one
to vie is to struggle for advantage

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'under' means further down the column, so the struggling ends up below the one — and that 'one' is the numeral, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivies are the climbers that smother walls and choke native growth, so 'invasive plants' defines them by the habit gardeners complain about.

clue.text: Hero of morality play, extremely beset by inversion of reputation

parts.note: your NAME is your reputation, written backwards
extremely and very are the same intensifier

explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an instruction to take outside letters, which is the trap — here it is only a synonym. The answer also names the Observer's own crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyman is the title character of the medieval morality play, summoned by Death, so the definition points at one named hero who stands for all of us.

clue.text: Phi taking opening to include reverse of popular device

parts.note: Phi is this setter's pen name, so he is ME
a chasm is a gaping opening in the ground
IN means popular, turned round

explanation.walkthrough: When a clue names the setter — Phi here — it almost always means ME or I. Bank that one: it turns an apparently impossible proper noun into two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mechanism is the working parts that make something go, so 'device' is a plain synonym taken at the machinery end of the word.

clue.text: Emptied kitchen provided with latest in fashionable kitchen tool?

parts.note: KitcheN with its insides scooped out
'provided' and 'if' introduce the same condition
the last letter of fashionablE

explanation.walkthrough: Kitchen appears twice and does a different job each time — first as letters to hollow out, then as half the definition. Spotting the repeat is the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A knife is the blade you chop and slice with, so 'kitchen tool' names it by the drawer it lives in rather than by any edge it has.

clue.text: Cumbrian river valley that's perceived back to front

parts.note: a dene is a narrow wooded valley
read literally: the letter at the back moves to the front

explanation.walkthrough: Cycling is not reversal — only the last letter travels, and the rest keep their order. A word that came back reversed would read ENED, which is nothing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eden rises in the Pennines and runs north through Carlisle to the Solway, so 'Cumbrian river' defines it by example.

clue.text: Dispensation of your pills including MDMA, with a degree of risk

indicators.note: anagram indicator — a dispensation hands things out

parts.note: anagram fodder
MDMA is ecstasy, and E is its street name

explanation.walkthrough: E for ecstasy is standard crossword shorthand, and 'dispensation' is both a pharmacy word and a shuffling instruction — the surface a chemist, the wordplay a drug deal.
explanation.definitionFit: Perilously means in a way that carries danger, so the adverbial phrase substitutes cleanly: 'balanced perilously' is 'balanced with a degree of risk'.

clue.text: Create place possibly from which article is taken — or where it may be stored?

parts.note: the letters the anagram works on
the indefinite article, and the letter taken out before the shuffle

explanation.walkthrough: The article is not something kept in the box but a letter to remove, and the dash is where the wordplay stops and the definition starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A receptacle is anything made to hold what you put in it, so 'where it may be stored' defines it by function rather than by shape or size.

clue.text: Concluding words about one French city

parts.note: an amen is the word that concludes a prayer
the Roman numeral one

explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here means around, not approximately — and the praying surface sits neatly on a city whose cathedral is the largest in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Amiens is the old capital of Picardy in northern France, so 'French city' defines it by example, one place standing for the category.

clue.text: Flowering plant: leave it to revert, surrounded by a lot of wood

parts.note: to leave is to go
deal is softwood board, and most of it is DEA
IT reverted

explanation.walkthrough: Deal is the timber trade's name for pine or fir board, and that piece of vocabulary is what the clue turns on; the colon does the work of 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Godetia is a garden annual grown for its papery pink and mauve blooms, so 'flowering plant' defines it by example — one genus for the class.

clue.text: NZ city almost recycled fabric

indicators.note: the closing N goes, leaving WELLINGTO

parts.note: Wellington is New Zealand's capital

explanation.walkthrough: 'Recycled' does two jobs at once: it sounds like reused cloth, and it asks for a cycle — letters travelling from one end to the other in their existing order.
explanation.definitionFit: Towelling is the looped cotton cloth that towels and dressing gowns are made of, so 'fabric' is a plain synonym for the material itself.

clue.text: Old King encountered old Queen — resistance showing here?

parts.note: O is the usual abbreviation for old
HM stands for His Majesty
encountered is met
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the previous monarch

explanation.walkthrough: ER for Elizabeth Regina is the crossword's default queen, and since Charles's accession she is the old one — which is also why HM is a king again.
explanation.definitionFit: An ohmmeter is the instrument that measures electrical resistance in ohms, so the definition describes it by what its dial displays.

clue.text: Husband keeps talking, dismissing foremost London team?

definitions.note: The Hammers is a plural nickname for a single club, so the definition counts one team while the answer counts the players it stands for.

indicators.note: the leading Y is dismissed, leaving AMMERS

parts.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
to yammer is to talk on and on

explanation.walkthrough: H for husband is a workhorse abbreviation, and the deletion is signalled by position rather than by letter: 'foremost' says which one goes, never what it is.
explanation.definitionFit: West Ham United are the Hammers, after the crossed hammers on the badge, so 'London team' picks the club out by example.

clue.text: America engaged in special survey, cut short, regarding the United States?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for special
a poll is a survey of opinion, docked of its last letter
the country's own initials

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the pun the clue turns on: marriage is a state of being united, and 'engaged' is quietly doing the same double work in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Spousal means of a husband or wife, and marriage is the state of being united — so the setter's 'United States' is matrimony, not America.

clue.text: Net trimmed aboard ship — backbreaking stuff?

definitions.note: The answer is plural where 'stuff' is a mass noun: straw is uncountable as a material, so the definition names the substance rather than counting stalks.

parts.note: SS, for steamship, is the crossword's standard vessel
a trawl is a net, trimmed here of its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the proverb: it is the last straw that breaks the camel's back. SS for ship is worth memorising — two letters that turn up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw only breaks a back in the saying about the camel, so 'backbreaking stuff' reaches the answer through that idiom rather than through any real weight.

clue.text: Lovers' encounter, initially under thoroughly wet part of church?

parts.note: to steep something is to soak it right through
the opening letters of Lovers and Encounter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Thoroughly wet' wants a verb, not an adjective — steep as in steeping tea — and in a down entry 'under' puts the initials at the foot of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tower and spire rising off a church roof, so 'part of church' names it by where it sits rather than what it does.

clue.text: Shun Italian guy doffing cap

indicators.note: the S at the head of the word comes off

parts.note: signore is Italian for gentleman or sir

explanation.walkthrough: Doffing a cap removes what sits on top, so it takes the first letter — and in a down entry that letter really is the topmost one.
explanation.definitionFit: To ignore someone is to behave as though they were not there, which is exactly what shunning does — the cold shoulder, without any formal expulsion.

clue.text: Athlete flailing another arm

indicators.note: anagram indicator — flailing limbs are out of control

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is exactly ten letters and so is the answer, which is the tell: count a suspected anagram against the enumeration before you commit to it.
explanation.definitionFit: A marathoner is someone who runs marathons, so 'athlete' defines by category — the general word standing over one very particular discipline.

clue.text: Drunken person leaving new parties on a mountain

parts.note: the letters to be shuffled
N is the abbreviation for new — the letter that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a mountaineering term and reads as a social one, which is where the clue hides; 'drunken' belongs to the wordplay, not to the party.
explanation.definitionFit: In climbing a rope is the group tied to a single line, so 'parties on a mountain' uses the mountaineers' own sense of the word rather than the cord.

clue.text: Give ear to piano in advertisement

parts.note: p is the musical direction for soft, short for piano
a lug is an ear in northern English

explanation.walkthrough: The clue asks you to listen, which is the last thing it means: 'give ear' is handing over a word for ear, and the piano is a marking on a score.
explanation.definitionFit: A plug is a free mention of a product on air or in print, so 'advertisement' takes the publicity sense, not the thing that stops a sink.

clue.text: Poor bats: upside down amid defoliation

definitions.note: The definition is plural and the answer singular because the tail is the cluster of weak batsmen at the end of an order — one word covering several players.

indicators.note: a down entry reads bottom to top, so the buried letters climb

parts.note: defoLIATion carries the letters, running the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The colon lets 'Poor bats' stand alone as the definition, and in a down entry 'upside down' is the honest way to say reversed: there is no backwards on a vertical axis.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket the tail is the last few batsmen, picked for their bowling, so 'poor bats' names them by the weakness everyone expects of them.

clue.text: Discussion subject in honour of film

parts.note: a toast in honour of someone is 'to' them
pic is the trade's short word for a picture

explanation.walkthrough: Pic for film comes out of the trade press, where a movie is a picture; the surface sounds like a film society and hides a plain two-part build.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is what a discussion is about, so 'discussion subject' is a plain synonym — the matter in hand rather than the talking itself.

clue.text: Bribe arranged in Ohio, offering notes in elevated positions?

parts.note: a sop is something handed over to placate someone
whoever ran an event arranged it
the clue's own 'in', taken as it stands
O is the old abbreviation for the state of Ohio

explanation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' looks like an instruction to shuffle and is not — it is a synonym for ran. Reaching for the anagram is exactly what the clue expects of you.
explanation.definitionFit: A sopranino is the smallest and highest instrument of its family, a recorder or a sax, so the definition describes it by the register it plays in.

clue.text: Philosopher's stratagem involving singular lines

parts.note: a ruse is a stratagem
s. is the grammarian's abbreviation for singular
l is a line, and doubling the letter makes it plural

explanation.walkthrough: Doubling an abbreviation to pluralise it — l and ll for lines, p and pp for pages — is a convention worth banking, because it turns up everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertrand Russell was the logician behind Principia Mathematica and a famous essayist, so 'Philosopher' defines him by example, one name for the profession.

clue.text: Poem's energy reflected in English crossword feature

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
the thing you are reading is a clue
GO is energy — 'plenty of go' — turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossword feature' pointing at the word clue is the setter winking at you, and GO for energy is the piece to remember: it turns up reversed as often as not.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclogue is a short pastoral poem in the tradition of Virgil, so 'Poem' defines it by class — the general word for a very particular kind.
